analysis.one_liner: Requires federal air and water pollution permits to account for combined pollution burdens and deny those that could harm community health.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in two House committees from October 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permitting rules so that regulators must look at the total pollution already burdening a neighborhood — from all sources, past and present — before issuing or renewing a permit. If adding a new or renewed facility's pollution could harm the general public or vulnerable groups like children, the elderly, or low-income residents, regulators would have to tighten the permit or deny it. It also required checks on companies with long records of violating environmental laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of overburdened communities — typically lower-income neighborhoods and communities of color that already host multiple pollution sources — who today face higher rates of asthma, cancer, and other illnesses. The bill's findings state that pollution's combined effects across many sources have been largely ignored in permitting decisions, and that children in these areas face lifelong consequences [S3]. Under the bill, the burden of proving no harm would shift from communities to polluting applicants [S3].

how_it_helps.text: EPA and state permitting authorities would have to analyze cumulative impacts — combined past, present, and foreseeable pollution in a geographic area — before issuing or renewing Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permits, and deny permits when there is no reasonable certainty of no harm to the general population or to susceptible subpopulations.

Permit applicants for major air sources would have to submit an analysis covering nearby schools, day care centers, nursing homes, hospitals, parks, and community demographics, and how their emissions combine with existing sources.

Companies deemed persistent violators of environmental law could be denied permits unless they submit an adequate compliance and community-consultation plan, and repeat offenders could be barred from renewal.
The bill's findings state that the burden of proving a proposed action will not harm communities should fall on polluting industries and the federal government, not the communities themselves.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities that hold or seek air and water pollution permits — such as chemical plants, refineries, power plants, and large wastewater dischargers, especially those located in or near already-polluted areas. They would bear the cost of preparing cumulative-impact analyses, installing additional controls, or losing permits outright if their combined contribution to neighborhood pollution could harm health.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed significant new analysis and compliance costs on permit applicants: major air sources must submit a cumulative impacts analysis covering demographics, exposure points, air, soil, water, and public health, and existing permits 3 years or longer would need revisions within 18 months of new rules.

The 'reasonable certainty of no harm' standard could deny or delay permits for facilities — including expansions that might otherwise bring jobs — in areas already carrying substantial pollution, and critics could argue the standard is so strict it effectively blocks new industrial activity in overburdened communities rather than managing it.

The bill would shift significant discretion to the EPA Administrator and state permitting authorities to determine harm at the census-block-group level, raising concerns about permitting uncertainty and administrative burden without clear scientific thresholds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes for communities that already carry disproportionate pollution are substantial, and the bill shifted the burden of proof onto polluters rather than residents. The costs fall on regulated industries, though some of those costs could translate into delayed projects or facility closures in affected areas. The bill never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to be tested in hearings or debate.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late October 2022 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Transportation and Infrastructure committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the Cumulative Impacts Act of 2022 in the House on October 21, 2022.

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and four days later to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change and the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial permit holders — particularly facilities located in already-polluted areas — are better off, since they never faced the new cumulative-impact analysis requirements, tighter permit conditions, or denial risk the bill would have created. Residents of overburdened communities remain subject to permitting decisions that, per the bill's own findings, do not account for combined pollution burdens [S3].

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cumulative Impacts Act of 2022 to require cumulative-impact analysis in Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act permitting.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 21, 2022 and referred it to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment; took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Industrial permit-holding sectors (chemical, refining, power, manufacturing, wastewater discharge)
against.what_they_did: The bill would have imposed new analysis, control, and permit-denial requirements on these sectors; no organized public support for the bill appears in the record, and it drew zero cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan alignment can be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Industrial air polluters (chemical plants, refineries, power plants, manufacturers)
industries.note: Major sources would have to submit cumulative-impact analyses covering nearby schools, hospitals, and demographics, and could have permits tightened or denied if combined neighborhood pollution threatens health. Existing permits would need revisions within 18 months of new rules.

industries.industry: Facilities holding Clean Water Act discharge permits
industries.note: Permit issuance and renewal would depend on a finding of reasonable certainty of no harm to the general population or susceptible subpopulations, considering existing water quality and combined discharges. States could block permits under the same standard.

Applicants deemed persistent violators could be denied permits outright unless they submit adequate compliance and community-consultation plans; a prior inadequate plan plus continued violations would bar renewal.
Mandatory cumulative-impact analyses for every major-source permit application would create demand for environmental assessment work. This is a secondary effect of the bill's public-health purpose.
